question: can an OWEM-style router beat any single model across all six axes?
answer: YES, by +10.6% — but only if it routes correctly more than 61.4% of the time.
THE_DECISIVE_NUMBER: 61.4%. A router that picks the right axis-specialist less often than that is WORSE than simply always using sov33-unified. The oracle gain of +0.069 is an UPPER BOUND that assumes perfect axis classification; a real router must first decide what kind of question it is looking at, and that classifier is itself error-prone. The economics are: at 70% routing accuracy the router gains +0.015, at 90% it gains +0.051.
THE_ROUTER_NEEDS_UNTRAINED_MODELS: 5 distinct models win at least one axis, and TWO OF THEM ARE UNTRAINED BASES — qwen2.5:1.5b wins conformance (0.636) and qwen2.5:0.5b wins continuity (0.462). An OWEM routing table built only from the trained sov line would be strictly worse than one that includes the stock models it was trained from.
WHAT_THIS_SAYS_ABOUT_sov34: sov34 scores 0.593 mean and wins exactly ONE of six axes — safety, where it is perfect at 1.000. sov33-unified scores 0.647 and wins two. On the six-axis mean, sov34 is THIRD, behind sov33-unified and behind stock llama3.2:3b. sov34 is a specialist, not a generalist, and the estate's framing of it as the flagship does not survive a six-axis mean.
limits: oracle scores come from a single 18-model run; no axis reaches usable_n>=30 so none of these per-axis figures is individually resolved, and the routing gain inherits that. The break-even accuracy is the robust part — it depends on the RATIO of oracle to misroute score, which is far less sensitive to per-axis noise than the levels are.
